Decision guide

An AI RFP template with a worked scoring example

An RFP for a ticket-triage pilot attracts three polished demos. Only one team explains what happens when a ticket arrives in the wrong language. A common test pack lets your reviewers reproduce the answer and compare the actual proposals.

Which bid wins the ticket-triage pilot?

Give both firms the same held-back tickets and ask one of your operators to trace a misroute using each firm’s handover notes. These fictional bids illustrate how to record what the panel saw.

Panel scores out of five
CriterionBid ABid B
Delivery5 · Routes every test ticket correctly.3 · Sends two multilingual tickets to the wrong queue.
Handover3 · The operator needs the bidder’s help to trace a failure.5 · The operator traces and replays a failure unaided.
Commercial clarity4 · Lists support hours. Exit work is unpriced.4 · Prices exit work. Extra support hours are unpriced.

Choose weights before inviting bids

For a pilot with supplier support, the example weights below give delivery 45%, handover 35% and commercial clarity 20%. Bid A earns 82/100 (45 + 21 + 16). Bid B earns 78/100 (27 + 35 + 16). The panel buys better routing but must budget staff time for assisted recovery.

For a different RFP where your team takes over on day one, giving handover 45% and delivery 35% reverses the result. B earns 82/100 and A earns 78/100. B’s handover advantage comes with two routing errors. Ask who will catch those tickets and how much rework they cause. Keep the published weights throughout each competition.

What goes in the award memo?

If buyer-owned repositories are mandatory and A has only promised access, record “A: 82, pending repository evidence.” Name the reviewer and the evidence needed to clear the condition. Record B’s eligibility separately. Ask each finalist for its missing price line before comparing total cost. A commercial clarity score measures how well the quote explains costs, not how low the price is.

The UK government’s AI procurement guidance asks buyers to consider ongoing support, whole-life cost and the team taking over maintenance. The weights and bid evidence here are illustrative. Read the UK government guidance.

Give every bidder the same starting material

Include a redacted process map, the allowed tools, a sample of representative tickets and the intended user. Reserve a few tickets for the live acceptance session. Ask the bidder to name the engineer and business owner responsible for each deliverable. Put assumptions and exclusions beside each price line.

Set mandatory conditions before scoring

If the buyer requires company-owned repositories or a particular data boundary, mark these as mandatory. A bidder that cannot demonstrate one has an open condition. Keep that condition visible even when the bidder scores well on a demo. Invite evidence of an equivalent solution if your procurement process permits one.

Calculate an example together

For this illustrative scorecard, score each dimension from zero to five, then multiply by its weight divided by five. A bid scoring four for delivery, three for operations and five for commercial clarity earns 36 + 21 + 20 = 77 points. Have reviewers attach their evidence independently before discussing a consensus score.

Illustrative buyer scenario

Two finalists, one unresolved condition

A selection panel likes one firm’s prototype. During the bid review, the panel discovers that the engineer who gave the demonstration is available only for discovery. The other bidder names its delivery lead and includes support but has a less polished demo.

Ask both finalists for the same staffing schedule, escalation contact and substitution terms. Before opening the revised prices, decide which staffing conditions are mandatory. Keep the panel’s original scores alongside the revised scores.

What to keep

A bid matrix with the quoted scope, evidence owner, open condition and the exact revision that resolved it.

When to pause

If a mandatory condition remains open, leave the bid pending. A strong presentation score cannot establish who will deliver the contracted work.

Make the decision

Use the award memo to explain the tradeoff the score hides. For example, a lower-scoring bid may still be viable if the team accepts a shorter pilot and a clear exit. Record the amendment and ask all eligible bidders the same clarification where your process requires it.
